V01-E-001: Lists of 'untranslatable' words circulate widely, each entry offering a term from some language for which English supposedly has no equivalent. The implication is usually that speakers of that language possess a feeling or concept that English speakers simply lack. But the lists themselves undercut the implication, since every entry is followed by a short English gloss that readers grasp at once. What such words reveal, then, is not a limit on what can be thought, only that one language has packed into a single word what another says in a phrase.
V01-E-002: Many historians believe that for long stretches of the past, reading was usually a spoken activity, with texts voiced to oneself or to a listening group. One reason was practical: books were scarce and costly, and a single copy read aloud could serve a whole household. Another lay in the page itself, since some early manuscripts ran their words together without spaces, and sounding them out helped readers find where each word ended. As books grew cheaper and pages easier to scan by eye, these reasons weakened, and the silent, solitary reader slowly became the norm.
V01-E-003: In face-to-face talk, a teasing remark is softened by a smile or a tone of voice that tells the listener it is not meant seriously. Written messages strip away these signals, which is why a brief text can read as curt or hostile when its writer intended nothing of the kind. Emoji added to the end of a message have come to fill part of this gap, marking a line as a joke, an apology or a friendly aside. Seen this way, they are less a new language than a set of written gestures, standing in for the face and voice that typed words leave behind. But like all gestures, they work only among people who read them the same way, which is why a message that delights one friend can puzzle another.
V01-E-004: Listeners asked to rate recordings of unfamiliar accents often judge some speakers more intelligent or trustworthy than others, though the recordings differ in nothing but pronunciation. A natural explanation is that certain accents simply sound clearer or more elegant, and that listeners are responding to qualities in the sound itself. Yet a pronunciation admired as refined in one region is often ridiculed as lazy in another, where a different group happens to use it. If the sound were doing the work, it should earn the same verdict everywhere; what varies with the verdict is the standing of the people heard using it. Judgements of accent, then, are largely judgements of speakers, which is why a once-mocked accent can rise in esteem when its speakers rise in the world.
V01-E-005: Street names look like neutral labels, chosen only so that letters arrive and visitors can find their way. In practice, many of them record what a city once wished to honour, whether a battle, a benefactor or a local hero. This is why renaming a street so often provokes argument, since removing a name can feel like withdrawing that honour. Some residents who object care mainly about the bother of changing their addresses, but the bitterest disputes are usually about memory rather than maps.
V01-E-006: Students who expect to teach material to others often learn it better than those who study it only to pass a test. Part of the reason is that preparing to explain something forces a learner to organise it, deciding what matters most and how the parts connect. It also exposes gaps, because an explanation that seemed clear in one's head tends to falter the moment it has to be spoken aloud. For these reasons, some teachers now ask pupils to explain a new idea to a partner before they practise it on their own.
V01-E-007: Open-book examinations are often assumed to be easy, as if allowing notes into the hall removed any need to study. Students who prepare on that assumption tend to discover their mistake within the first hour, leafing through pages for answers that are printed nowhere. Such answers are missing because a well-set paper of this kind asks not what a theorem states, which the book would supply, but when it applies and what follows from it. The format does not lower the demand on students so much as move it, from remembering material to knowing how to use it.
V01-E-008: In many multilingual countries, children begin school in a language they rarely hear at home, on the theory that early immersion is the quickest route to fluency. The theory has intuitive appeal, but it overlooks what a child must accomplish in the first years of school besides acquiring a language. Those years are when children learn to read, to reason with numbers and to ask questions, and each of these is harder in a language they only half understand. A child taught first in the home language can build these skills on secure ground and later carry them over into the second language. Far from delaying the second language, then, the home language becomes the bridge by which a child crosses into it.
V01-E-009: Students who type their lecture notes can usually record far more of what is said than students who write by hand. That speed, however, tempts typists to take down the lecturer's words almost verbatim, without pausing to think about them. Those writing by hand cannot keep up, and so they are forced to choose what matters and to put it into their own words. This selection and rephrasing is a form of thinking about the material, which may be why handwritten notes, though shorter, are sometimes remembered better.
V01-E-010: For beginners in algebra, studying a fully worked solution is often more instructive than attempting the same problem unaided. Lacking the patterns that would guide them, they spend their attention on fruitless search and have little left for noticing why a method works. Learners who already command the patterns are in the opposite position, since every worked step repeats what they could have supplied themselves. For them, reading the solution becomes a distraction, and attempting the problem unaided is the better exercise.
V01-E-011: Patients warned that a drug may cause headaches or nausea report those symptoms more often than patients given no warning, even when their pills contain no active ingredient. This nocebo effect places doctors in an awkward position, because the duty to inform patients of risks seems to produce some of the very harms described. Withholding the warnings is hardly an answer, since it would sacrifice the patient's right to decide about treatment with full knowledge. A more promising approach is to change how risks are framed, for instance by noting that most people taking the drug feel no side effects at all.
V01-E-012: Surgical teams are made up of highly trained people, so it can seem odd to ask them to work through a simple checklist before an operation. Yet many surgical errors arise not from ignorance but from small omissions, such as failing to confirm which side of the body is to be operated on. These are exactly the steps that experts, working under pressure and confident in their routine, are most likely to skip. A checklist catches such lapses by making the routine explicit and requiring each member of the team to confirm it aloud. Its value, then, lies not in teaching surgeons anything new but in protecting what they already know from ordinary failures of attention.
V01-E-013: A large share of patients prescribed long-term medicines stop taking them sooner than their doctors intended. This is often blamed on forgetfulness, yet many of those who stop do so deliberately, and for reasons that seem sound from where they stand. A patient taking a drug for high blood pressure, for example, may feel no different with it than without it, and conclude that the pills are doing nothing. Given that experience, stopping is a reasonable inference rather than a lapse, which suggests that the remedy lies less in reminders than in explanation.
V01-E-014: People who report persistent loneliness tend, on average, to be in poorer health than people who do not. It would be rash to conclude from this alone that loneliness causes illness, since illness can itself confine people to their homes and thin out their social lives. Studies that follow the same people over many years help here, because they can check whether loneliness at the start predicts illness that was not yet present. Where it does, the reverse explanation cannot be the whole story, and loneliness deserves attention as a possible cause of ill health rather than merely its by-product.
V01-E-015: When a city proposes closing a shopping street to cars, the loudest objections usually come from the shopkeepers who trade on it. Their fear is understandable: customers who cannot park outside, they reason, will simply take their custom elsewhere. Yet traders often overestimate how many of their customers arrive by car, and underestimate how much those on foot spend over repeated visits. A street that is pleasant to linger in can therefore gain trade, although the gain is likeliest where enough people already live or work within walking distance.
V01-E-016: Many cities have installed benches with armrests spaced along their length or seats tilted at an uncomfortable angle. Such designs are usually justified as ways of keeping public seating available to everyone who needs it. In practice, their chief effect is to stop people from lying down, which means they are aimed above all at those with nowhere else to sleep. Critics argue that this moves a social problem out of sight without doing anything to solve it.
V01-E-017: Before railways and paved roads, a mountain range could be crossed by loaded animals at only a few places where the terrain allowed it. Traders from a wide region were therefore funnelled through the same narrow passes, whatever their origin or destination. Settlements at the foot of such passes could profit handsomely, supplying fresh animals, lodging and guides to every caravan that came through. The same concentration made them targets, however, since whoever held a pass could tax or block all the traffic that depended on it. The wealth of a pass town was thus never secure, resting as it did on a position that others had every reason to covet.
V01-E-018: No flat map can show the curved surface of the earth without distortion; it can keep shapes true over small regions, or keep areas true, but never both at once. Every projection is therefore a choice about which property to sacrifice, and the right choice depends on what the map is meant to do. The projection long used for sea charts shows what such a choice involves: it keeps compass directions true, so that a sailor can follow a straight line on the chart at a constant bearing. The price is that lands far from the equator are drawn much larger than they really are, an exaggeration that grows steadily towards the poles. To fault the chart's makers for this exaggeration is to forget what the chart was for, though the fault is real when a navigator's tool hangs on classroom walls as a picture of the world.
V01-E-019: Many people feel that deceiving someone with a carefully chosen truth is less wrong than telling an outright lie. Asked whether a used car has given trouble, a seller who replies that 'it passed its inspection last month' may avoid any false statement while concealing a history of breakdowns. The buyer who trusts that answer ends up exactly as deceived, and exactly as much out of pocket, as one who had been told a direct falsehood. If the difference matters at all, it must lie in something other than the harm done, perhaps in how much of the work of being misled is left to the listener.
V01-E-020: Paternalism is the practice of restricting people's choices for their own good, as when a law requires riders of motorcycles to wear helmets. Its defenders point out that people often choose badly when risks seem remote, and that a small restriction can prevent a great deal of suffering. Its critics reply that adults have a right to run risks with their own lives, even foolish ones, and that a state deciding their good for them treats them as children. Since neither side holds its view without exception, much of the debate turns on where to draw the line: few would ban mountain climbing, yet few object to warning labels on poisonous medicines.
V01-E-021: It is widely held that a person should be judged only for what lay within their control. Two hikers who each toss a lit match into dry grass are, on this principle, equally culpable, whatever happens next. Suppose one match fizzles out harmlessly while the other starts a blaze that destroys a neighbouring farm. Almost no one would then judge the two alike: the hiker whose match caught is condemned, and punished, far more severely than the other. The case leaves us choosing between a principle that seems obviously right and a response that seems just as hard to give up.
V01-E-022: It is often said that we owe obligations to people who will live centuries from now, though they cannot thank us or hold us to account. A puzzle arises because many of our larger choices, about where to build or how to use resources, will affect which particular people come to be born at all. A person who owes her very existence to such a choice can hardly complain that it harmed her, since without it she would never have lived. If the obligation survives this puzzle, it must be owed not to particular future individuals but to whoever comes to live, as a duty to leave them a world worth inheriting.
V01-E-023: Once we understand something well, it becomes surprisingly hard to imagine what it was like not to understand it. This is why experts so often make poor teachers of beginners, skipping steps that seem too obvious to mention. The steps are obvious only to them, however, because their own knowledge fills the gaps without their noticing. A useful remedy is to try an explanation on someone new to the subject, who will stumble exactly where the hidden steps were left out.
V01-E-024: People who have just been given a mug typically ask more to part with it than people without one will offer for an identical mug. The gap is puzzling on a simple view of value, since a few minutes of ownership cannot have made the mug any more useful. One explanation is that giving something up registers as a loss, and losses weigh more heavily with us than gains of the same size. On this account, owner and buyer are not really pricing the same thing, since the owner is weighing the loss of a mug and the buyer the gain of one. Their figures differ, then, because they are answering different questions, and neither need be mistaken about the mug itself.
V01-E-025: Chronic delay is commonly diagnosed as a failure of planning, and the usual cures are calendars, deadlines and lists. The diagnosis fits poorly those habitual delayers who can say exactly when a task is due and how long it will take, yet put it off regardless. Their difficulty is that the task stirs boredom, self-doubt or fear of judgement, and delay relieves these feelings at once, while its costs arrive only later. Remedies that merely improve the schedule leave this bargain intact, which may be why some people keep buying new planners without delaying any less.
